extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: A sample patent-eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101) rejection applying the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG) to claims reciting computer-implemented steps, showing how to identify an abstract idea and analyze whether additional elements supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 statutory baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the statutory language as the baseline for patentable subject matter. Claims must be considered against this statutory text when determining eligibility under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea — Mental Processes grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, covers performance of the limitation in the mind but for the recitation of generic computer components, then it falls within the 'Mental Processes' grouping of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the limitation (e.g., 'determining the amount of use of each icon' or 'ranking the icons based on the determined amount of use') could be performed manually or mentally. Examples: without 'by a processor', 'determining' could encompass a user manually calculating usage; 'ranking' could encompass a user thinking which icons are most used. If so, treat the limitation as an abstract idea in the Mental Processes category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation for mental-process analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements should be given their broadest reasonable interpretation to determine whether, absent the recitation of generic computer components, they cover activity that can be performed in the human mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip away generic computer-language (e.g., 'by a processor') when testing whether the recited step could reasonably be performed mentally. If the limitation still reads as a mental step, it supports classification as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (significantly more test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the judicial exception (abstract idea) is integrated into a practical application; additional claim elements must do more than nominally recite generic technology and must impose meaningful limits on practicing the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that only adds a generic computer performing the abstract idea at a high level does not integrate the exception into a practical application. Look for elements that provide a technical solution, improve computer functionality, or impose concrete limits on how the abstract idea is applied. If additional elements 'amount to no more than mere instructions to apply the exception using a generic computer component,' they do not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components recited at a high level are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a processor (or other generic computer components) at a high level of generality, performing generic computer functions, amounts to mere instructions to apply the abstract idea using a generic computer and does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim's only additional element is 'using a processor' to perform abstract-idea steps (e.g., ranking and determining), that high-level recitation 'does not impose any meaningful limits' and therefore cannot transform the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter. Examiners should reject claims that add only such generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply the exception cannot provide an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of mere instructions to apply an abstract idea using a generic computer component cannot provide an inventive concept sufficient for patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether any claimed element contributes something more than conventional or generic implementation. If the claimed additional elements simply tell a practitioner to implement the abstract idea on a computer without more, they fail to supply the required 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for §101 rejections (procedural guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sample rejection uses form paragraphs 7.04.01, 7.05, and 7.05.016 and inserts appropriate explanatory language for the 2019 PEG analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Office procedures by using the cited form paragraphs when drafting §101 rejections under the 2019 PEG and insert tailored explanations as shown in the sample. This is a procedural requirement to ensure uniformity and completeness in rejection wording.
